params.title: Power Sources
params.subtitle: GMDSS batteries, chargers and the reserve source of energy, plus linear and switching power supplies and their protection.

onScreen: Batteries, chargers, the reserve source of energy and power supplies
scenes.narration: This lesson is about power for the GMDSS, the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System. We'll cover the batteries, how they're charged, and the reserve source of energy that keeps the radios on the air when ship's power fails. Then we'll look inside power supplies: rectifiers, filters, switching supplies and their protection circuits. First, the battery cells themselves.

params.title: Normal cell voltages
rows: Building block of the GMDSS bank

scenes.narration: Each NICAD, or nickel-cadmium, battery cell has a normal voltage of 1.2 volts. Don't confuse it with 1.5 volts: that belongs to dry cells. Each lead acid battery cell has a normal voltage of 2.1 volts. So a 12 volt battery has 6 cells: 6 times 2.1 is 12.6 volts. And a 24 volt GMDSS battery bank has 12 cells.

callouts.label: Measure the electrolyte with a hydrometer, not a voltmeter
Fully charged lead acid cell: specific gravity 1.280
Higher temperature: lower reading, though the charge is unchanged
Gel cell: sealed, so special charging rates and voltages may be needed

scenes.narration: To check a lead acid cell's state of charge, measure its electrolyte with a hydrometer, not a voltmeter. The normal specific gravity of a fully charged lead acid cell is 1.280. Watch the temperature, though. A higher temperature results in a lower specific gravity reading, because warm electrolyte expands and becomes less dense, even though the state of charge hasn't changed. And gel cell batteries are typically sealed: they're lead acid, with the electrolyte held as a gel. So special charging rates and voltages may be required.

onScreen: Discharge current charges it in reverse polarity
scenes.narration: Picture a string of cells in a battery, discharging. What happens if one cell becomes weaker than the remaining cells? The same discharge current still has to flow through every cell. So the discharge current of the remaining cells effectively charges the weaker cell in reverse polarity, all while the battery feeds its load. That's another reason to keep every cell equally charged, which brings us to battery chargers.

onScreen: Ship's main and emergency power feed the charger
Reserve Source of Energy: when both fail
Float and trickle are charge rates, not modes
scenes.narration: Now the GMDSS power system. Normally the ship's power feeds a GMDSS compliant battery charger, which supplies the radio installation. The Reserve Source of Energy is power to operate the radio installation and conduct Distress and Safety communications if the ship's main and emergency sources of electrical power fail. It is not the emergency generator. The charger has 3 modes. Charging keeps the battery charged. Change-over switches the radio load to the battery when ship's power fails. Parallel has the charger and battery feeding the load together. Float and trickle are charge rates, not these modes.

badges.label: Standard lead acid battery
badges.note: Until the gassing range: every cell equally full

badges.label: At the gassing range
badges.note: Inhibits electrolytic gas, then switches to float

badges.label: Maintenance free gel batteries
badges.note: Set during setup: sealed cells can't vent gas

onScreen: High charge once a week, to the gassing range
Then interrupt high charge and float
Gel batteries: high charge disabled at setup
scenes.narration: With a standard lead acid battery and a fully automatic GMDSS compliant charger, high charging is used once a week until the battery reaches the gassing range. That brings every cell to an equal full charge. Then the automatic charger interrupts the high charging process to inhibit the generation of electrolytic gas, and switches to float. Maintenance free lead acid gel batteries are different. During setup, the high, or Full, charging mode must be disabled, because sealed gel cells cannot vent gas or have water added.

params.title: Reading the console voltmeter
params.formula: Volts per cell = meter reading ÷ cells
steps: 24 VDC GMDSS station: 12 lead acid cells
Charger stuck in high charge: overcharging
params.answer: Constant 30 V: a fault. Brief high reading: normal

onScreen: Brief high reading after a battery test: normal
scenes.narration: On a 24 volt DC, or direct current, GMDSS station, keep an eye on the console voltmeter. The battery has 12 lead acid cells. A constant 30 volt reading indicates a malfunction. Divide it out: 30 volts over 12 cells is 2.5 volts per cell. That means the charger is stuck in high charge and overcharging the battery. Don't mistake a normal reading for a fault, though. After testing the station on battery power, a brief high voltage reading, or a high charge current that then declines, is normal, not a malfunction.

blocks.label: Full wave rectifier
blocks.note: 2 or more diodes; bridge: no center tap

blocks.label: DC output
blocks.note: Ripple at 120 Hz: twice the input

onScreen: Full wave rectifier: more than 1 diode
120 Hz ripple: twice the input frequency
scenes.narration: Now power supplies. A standard full wave rectifier power supply starts with an AC, or alternating current, input, here at 60 hertz. Full wave rectifiers always use more than 1 diode, and a bridge rectifier needs no center tapped transformer secondary. The rectifier uses both halves of each input cycle, so there are 2 pulses per input cycle. After the rectifier comes the filter, which smooths the pulses into DC. What's left is ripple, and its frequency is twice the input frequency: a 60 hertz input gives 120 hertz ripple.

onScreen: Peak currents: choke low, capacitive high
Output: choke relatively low, capacitive higher
scenes.narration: There are 2 kinds of input filter to compare, row by row. Voltage regulation: an inductive, or choke, input filter gives good regulation, and a capacitive input gives poor regulation. Transformer utilization factor: high for the choke input. Rectifier peak currents: low for the choke input, high for the capacitive input. Output voltage: relatively low for the choke input. A capacitive input charges toward the peak voltage, so its output is higher.

params.title: Switcher type power supply
rows: Line voltage directly rectified and filtered
Increased complexity: more likely to fail
Tends to create radiated RF, not AF

scenes.narration: Now the switcher type power supply, its advantages and disadvantages side by side. Its first advantage: the line voltage itself, not a transformed voltage, is directly rectified and filtered to produce a high DC voltage. Against that, increased complexity, which means more likelihood of a component failure. Next, its components are much smaller and lighter weight, but the cost goes up, because there are many more parts. Finally, it can provide much better efficiency, but it has a tendency to create radiated RF, or radio frequency energy, not AF, audio frequency.

blocks.label: Inverter (chopper)
blocks.note: Chops the DC at high frequency

onScreen: Output transformer with a ferrite core
Output rectifier and filter to DC output
Feedback loop to the chopper controller and inverter
scenes.narration: Here's the configuration of a mains operated switching power supply with output regulation. The mains go to the input rectifier and filter. The inverter, or chopper, chops that DC at high frequency into the output transformer. Switching power supply transformers use a ferrite core to reduce losses at high frequencies, not a laminated steel core. Then come the output rectifier and filter. Regulation comes from a chopper controller: a feedback loop runs from the DC output back to the controller, which drives the inverter to hold the output steady.

params.title: Duty cycle: the switch's on time
labels: On for half of each period: a 50% duty cycle
A BUCK supply steps the voltage down in proportion to the duty cycle
Its output never exceeds its input

onScreen: BUCK: steps voltage down in proportion to duty cycle
scenes.narration: Now the buck switching power supply. Its switch turns on and off rapidly, and the duty cycle is the fraction of each period the switch is on. Here it's on for half of each period, a 50 percent duty cycle. A buck supply steps the voltage down in proportion to the duty cycle. Since the switch can't be on for more than the whole period, a buck output never exceeds its input.

params.title: BUCK supply: 10 volts in
params.answer: V<sub>out</sub> = 5 V: 10 volts in, 5 volts out

onScreen: V out = duty cycle × V in
scenes.narration: Let's work the numbers. V sub out equals the duty cycle times V sub in. Take a 50 percent duty cycle, which is 0.5, and an input of 10 volts. V sub out is 0.5 times 10 volts, which is 5 volts. So 10 volts in gives 5 volts out. Raise or lower the duty cycle and the output follows, but it never goes above the input.

params.title: Protection and the truth about switchers
items: Crowbar: shorts the output on overvoltage, blowing the fuse or tripping the current limit
"No RFI problems" is not a switcher advantage: fast switching creates interference
Real advantages: wide input voltage range, works on DC input, lighter than linear supplies
Input current: short pulses near the AC peaks, high harmonic content, low power factor

onScreen: Crowbar: shorts the output on overvoltage
"No RFI problems" is not an advantage
Wide input range, DC input, lighter weight
High harmonic content, low power factor
scenes.narration: Protection first. The function of a crowbar circuit is to prevent an overvoltage condition from damaging circuitry. It shorts the power supply output, which blows the fuse or trips the current limit. Now a trap. No RFI problems is not an advantage of a switching power supply. RFI means radio-frequency interference, and fast switching creates it. The real advantages include working with a wide range of input voltages, working with direct current input, and lighter weight than linear power supplies. Finally, switching mode power supply input current has high harmonic content and a low power factor, because it is drawn in short pulses near the AC peaks.
